How do we run LangChain/LLamaIndex agents with prefix caching?

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-09-14
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Li (Redwood SE), Jared Morales (CTO - Nebula), Priya Shah (Lead ML), Samir Gupta (Platform), Lena Ortiz (Security)

Summary (auto): Intent: evaluate integration approach. Focus on onramp proxy that handles auth, routing, rate limits, observability - to centralize vendor calls.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, appreciate it. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Jared (Nebula CTO): Jared here.
[00:07] Priya: Priya.
[00:09] Samir: Samir.
[00:10] Lena: Lena.
[00:12] Connor (Redwood SE): Connor from Redwood.
[00:14] Maya: Great. I'll kick off with context on Redwood and then Connor will take the deep integration stuff. We sent the short primer but want to focus on your onramp idea.
[00:28] Jared: High level - we're trying to standardize LLM calls across product teams. A lot of teams are using LangChain or LlamaIndex locally with different providers, and ops wants a single gateway so we can control quotas and observability.
[00:45] Priya: Yes and also we need predictable p95 latency, and some teams want the lowest cost path for embeddings. We're evaluating hosted, dedicated, and private deployment.
[00:58] Connor: Makes sense. From an architecture perspective there are two common approaches: 1) clients call Redwood's SDK/hosted endpoint directly (we handle routing, KMS, SSO), or 2) you run an internal onramp / proxy which forwards to Redwood and centralizes policy. Both are valid.
[01:15] Samir: We're leaning toward the onramp because we want to inject request metadata and do token accounting before it leaves our network.
[01:23] Maya: Perfect. Connor can walk through an example pattern with LangChain and a sidecar proxy.
[01:30] Connor: Cool. So imagine a small sidecar (or a central gateway) that exposes the same API surface as Redwood SDK. Your services and LangChain agents point to the proxy. The proxy is responsible for auth (internal SSO tokens), per-route rate limits, caching of common prompts or prefixes, and observability hooks - emitting traces and token counts to Datadog/Prometheus.
[01:55] Priya: Quick question - for LangChain and LlamaIndex, do we need to change the chains or retrievers? We want to avoid a heavy rewrite.
[02:03] Connor: You shouldn't need to change chain logic. Most folks set the LLM client base_url to point at the proxy. For LlamaIndex you can swap the client endpoint similarly. There are minor header expectations — like X-Project-ID or our Redwood routing header — but no code changes to chain steps.
[02:20] Jared: Ok. What about streaming responses? We rely on streaming for chat latency.
[02:26] Connor: We support streaming over the SDK and the proxy can stream--we proxy chunked responses. There's a little extra latency from the hop, but it's usually single-digit ms if the proxy is colocated.
[02:36] Samir: Colocated meaning same VPC or same AZ?
[02:39] Connor: Same VPC or AZ preferred. If you're running the proxy in your VPC and Redwood's Private deployment is in your region, latency is minimal. For Hosted, you still get good numbers but it depends on egress and peering.
[02:50] Priya: How do we handle KV cache and prefix caching? We use KV to store conversation caches for retrieval-augmented generation.
[02:58] Connor: Redwood has automatic KV/prefix caching options available at the runtime; the proxy can also serve as a caching layer. If you want consistent caching across requests, running the cache inside the proxy (or pointing to a shared Redis) is common. Note: our runtime's KV cache is optimized for token-level reuse which reduces per-token cost.
[03:20] Lena (Security): On compliance - we're SOC 2 bound. We need audit trails, customer-managed keys, and proof that PII doesn't leak. How does Redwood handle KMS?
[03:30] Maya: Good question. For Private deployments you can bring your own KMS and HSM integrations. For Dedicated there's a managed KMS offering with BYOK options and audit logs. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer keys and audit exports. We'll send the KMS integration doc in the follow up.
[03:46] Lena: And logs? We need per-request audit logs exported to our logging infra.
[03:51] Connor: We can ship structured trace and request metadata via webhook or push to your S3, and we also support pushing metrics and spans to Datadog and Prometheus via exporters. Audit logs include model id, route, token counts, and redaction markers.
[04:05] Priya: Can we turn off storage of prompts on Redwood's side? Some teams want zero retention.
[04:12] Maya: Yes, retention is configurable. For Private you control retention fully. For Hosted/Dedicated we offer no-persist modes and per-route retention settings. We'll include the retention matrix in the packet.
[04:22] Jared: On rate limits - we need per-team quotas and a global burst bucket. Can Redwood apply different rate limits per route and per API key?
[04:32] Connor: Yes. Redwood supports hierarchical rate limiting: key-level, route-level, and project-level. You can also configure quota windows and burst capacity for important routes. The proxy can enforce token-based quotas before traffic reaches Redwood if you prefer pre-filtering.
[04:46] Samir: How do you count tokens for quotas? Are we billed for input+output? We want the quota to reflect cost.
[04:54] Connor: We provide token accounting (input + output) and have token-level billing metrics. The proxy can report token estimates pre-call if clients want to prevent exceeding quotas. That estimate is good to within a small variance depending on tokenizer differences.
[05:08] Priya: Are SDKs available in Python and Node? And is there a LangChain connector maintained?
[05:14] Maya: Yes, official SDKs in Python, Node, and Go. We maintain a LangChain connector repo with examples for chat, retrieval-augmented generation, and streaming. We'll share links.
[05:25] Priya: Nice. Any recommended best practices for LlamaIndex specifically?
[05:28] Connor: For LlamaIndex you generally point the LLMPredictor or service context to the proxy endpoint. Use chunking and embedding batching. For embeddings we recommend batched calls to reduce overhead; Redwood has batched embedding endpoints that we can route to cheaper variants.
[05:44] Jared: Cheaper variants meaning quantized models?
[05:47] Connor: Exactly—model variants that are quantized or have lower context windows. Our smart routing can route embeddings and generation to different model families based on route policy.
[05:55] Samir: Observability—what exact hooks do we get? We want token-level metrics, per-route latency, skew in p95, and traces that tie to our request IDs.
[06:05] Connor: You get token counts, per-model latency histogram, per-route and per-key quotas, error codes with stack, and full traces. The proxy can inject your internal request-id header (x-req-id) and Redwood traces will include it so you can correlate in your APM. We also export span links for sampled traces.
[06:22] Priya: Does Redwood emit metrics to Prometheus or is it push-only?
[06:26] Connor: Both—Prometheus pull metrics for on-prem/private setups and push to a metrics gateway for hosted. For Datadog we have a direct integration and we can ship logs + traces there.
[06:36] Lena: For security review, we will need to run a pen-test and see timeline for private deployment.
[06:41] Maya: We support security assessments; Private deployments are often packaged for air-gap validation. We also provide SOC2 artifacts and can coordinate an NDA for any deep work.
[06:52] Jared: Great. Priya, can you describe the workload we plan to bench?
[06:55] Priya: Sure — primary workload is a chat assistant (multi-turn) used on our support portal. Typical prompt size 400 tokens input, 350 output. Concurrent sessions at peak ~200 QPS across teams, P95 target 300ms on generation-only requests (excl network). Embeddings workload is a nightly batch of ~3M docs for index refresh.
[07:21] Connor: Useful. For the chat workload, we recommend dedicated capacity if keeping p95 under 300ms is critical and you want predictable infra. Hosted can hit that sometimes but depends on region and noise. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable KV cache locality.
[07:39] Samir: If we go dedicated, is there a managed upgrade/rollout tool? We want zero-downtime rollouts for model version updates.
[07:46] Connor: Yes—rollouts are supported with canaries and automatic fallback to previous model variants. You can pin versions and route a percentage of traffic. The runtime supports per-route rollout policies.
[07:56] Jared: About the proxy, does Redwood have a reference repo for the onramp?
[07:59] Connor: We do. It's a lightweight Go/Node sidecar that handles auth exchange (OIDC), key rotation, per-route rate limiting, and telemetry forwarding. We also have Kubernetes helm charts and a sample mesh config for Istio/Envoy if you prefer sidecar mesh.
[08:17] Priya: Do you support a gateway pattern where the proxy rewrites requests for longer context windows into chunked calls? We have some cases where we want to stream long files into the model.
[08:27] Connor: We have a chunking helper in the SDK that will split long inputs and stitch outputs. The proxy can orchestrate that to avoid client complexity. It can also cache intermediate embeddings to accelerate repeated reads.
[08:40] Samir: Rate-limits on chunked operations — do you expose them as a single logical call or multiple billable calls?
[08:47] Connor: From billing/token accounting perspective it's per model invocation, so chunked calls will sum. But we can expose a logical view in metrics so you see per-high-level-request totals. The proxy can present that aggregated number to your internal dashboards.
[09:00] Jared: Any gotchas with tokenizer differences across model families?
[09:04] Connor: There can be variance. We provide tokenizer estimate functions in the SDK. For strict quotas you should run a small compatibility validation during pilot. That's part of the bench plan we'll run.
[09:16] Priya: What's typical time to start a small POC on Dedicated? We want to test both Dedicated and Hosted with the proxy.
[09:22] Maya: For a sandbox dedicated test—if you commit to a short-term reserved capacity it can be provisioned in a few days. Hosted tests you can start immediately. Private (VPC) deployment typically takes longer — often 4–6 weeks including networking and KMS integration.
[09:40] Lena: For Private, do you require inbound connections from Redwood or is control plane customer-hosted?
[09:46] Connor: Private gives you a customer-managed control plane in most deployments. We support both models—pull-only egress or peered control plane depending on your security posture. We'll share the deployment options doc.
[09:57] Samir: How do we handle model updates if we're using a private offload?
[10:01] Connor: You can pin model versions. Updates are opt-in and we provide signed images and release notes. There's also an offline update path for air-gapped sites.
[10:11] Jared: Let's talk SLA: 99.95? What are realistic uptime and latency guarantees for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[10:18] Maya: Dedicated gets SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; hosted has best-effort plus credits. We'll include SLA details in the packet. Specific latency targets are attached to capacity commitments.
[10:27] Priya: For the bench, can we simulate our exact prompt distribution?
[10:30] Connor: Yes — please provide the prompt set and distribution. We'll run p95/p99 tests with similar concurrency and token distribution. We'll also test cold vs warm KV cache scenarios.
[10:41] Priya: We'll include retention rules and a couple of sample assistant conversations.
[10:44] Maya: Good. A few more quick things — error handling and backpressure. If Redwood returns 429/overquota, can the proxy add retry/backoff and circuit-breaker logic?
[10:53] Connor: Absolutely. The proxy should implement client-facing quota feedback; for 429s we recommend returning clear error codes to callers and doing exponential backoff. The proxy can also queue non-latency-sensitive tasks to a background worker for retries.
[11:05] Samir: Observability again — is there a single schema for events so our SIEM can ingest?
[11:09] Connor: We emit structured JSON events with fields: request_id, project_id, api_key_id, model_id, route, token_count_input, token_count_output, duration_ms, status_code. That's consumable by SIEMs.
[11:23] Priya: Will the trace include the individual model shard or GPU id? We want help debugging slow requests.
[11:29] Connor: Traces can include runtime node metadata at a coarse level — region, pool id, instance type, and approximate queueing time. We avoid exposing low-level host identifiers in hosted mode for security, but Dedicated/Private can surface more detail.
[11:43] Jared: How do you think about multi-tenant isolation on Dedicated?
[11:47] Connor: Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools; workloads are reserved. We also offer RBAC and route-level ACLs so teams only access their routes. For strict isolation we recommend Private.
[11:58] Priya: Any rate-limiting rules you recommend for chat vs embeddings?
[12:03] Connor: Chat is typically latency-sensitive so lower per-request quotas but higher concurrency; embeddings are throughput oriented so you might want batch quotas and larger burst allowances. We'll work with you to tune the quota windows.
[12:16] Maya: Can I pause and ask about pricing model? Jared earlier said cost sensitivity is big.
[12:20] Jared: Yes — we want to understand unit economics for chat vs embeddings.
[12:25] Maya: Unit pricing is by token for generation and per-embedding call for embeddings, with dedicated reserved capacity discounts. We'll send an example TCO sheet modeling your 3M doc embedding refresh.
[12:36] Priya: For embeddings, can you recommend an embedding model balanced for quality and cost?
[12:40] Connor: We can recommend a family tuned for quality/cost tradeoffs. There's also quantized embedding variants that save cost at slight quality delta. We'll include sample eval metrics.
[12:50] Samir: Are there any existing customers using a similar proxy approach you can point to?
[12:55] Maya: We have a few anonymized case studies where customers run a sidecar and do central orchestration—I'll include those links.
[13:03] Jared: On the bench, we want to ensure we test auto-failover if an AZ goes down. How does Redwood handle region failovers?
[13:11] Connor: Smart routing will fallback to a compatible model variant in another region. You can define policy to only route within region for data residency, or allow cross-region fallback for resilience.
[13:24] Priya: Ok, quick off-topic: do you support function-calling or tool invocation in the SDKs?
[13:29] Connor: Yes, function/tool calling patterns are supported. The SDK includes helpers for structured output and validation.
[13:36] Samir: Do we get structured output logs? We want to index tool calls.
[13:40] Connor: Tool calls are included in trace events with their input/output; they can be redacted for PII.
[13:46] Jared: Great. Time check — we have about 35 minutes left. Let's dive into a rough plan: Priya will share prompts by 9/18; Maya sends pricing by 9/16; Connor sets up bench plan.
[13:59] Priya: Sounds good. A few more technical clarifications. For the proxy sample repo, what's the recommended auth pattern for internal services? OIDC? mTLS?
[14:08] Connor: Both are supported. We recommend OIDC for service identity and mTLS for intra-cluster security if you already use it. The proxy can validate tokens and rotate credentials to Redwood.
[14:18] Samir: Are API keys rotated automatically on Redwood?
[14:21] Connor: Keys can be rotated; we also have short-lived tokens via OIDC token exchange which we recommend for internal proxies to avoid managing long-lived secrets.
[14:33] Priya: When we do the bench, can we test a mixed workload — chat QPS with embedding refresh concurrently?
[14:37] Connor: Yes, we'll create a mixed workload scenario and show how dedicated capacity allocation can be partitioned.
[14:45] Jared: One more, for debugging, will we get sample spans correlated to requests and model traces?
[14:51] Connor: Yes — we'll provide trace correlation examples.
[14:55] Maya: Quick call-out — we've seen customers set an internal quota guard in the proxy that will drop expensive requests above a threshold rather than flood Redwood; it helps control costs.
[15:04] Priya: That's interesting — a soft throttle would be useful.
[15:07] Samir: Ok, any blockers from our side to start the POC?
[15:10] Priya: Just getting the prompt set and network egress rules documented. Samir will confirm firewall and egress constraints.
[15:17] Samir: I'll get that by next Tuesday.
[15:20] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the packet and links. Any final questions?
[15:25] Lena: Only that we'll want a short security deep-dive next week once we review the docs.
[15:29] Maya: Noted. We'll schedule a security review with the SRE/security team.
[15:33] Jared: Thanks all. Recap?
[15:36] Maya: Recap — 1) Maya sends pricing + SOC2 + KMS notes by 9/16; 2) Connor prepares bench plan and sidecar repo links by 9/22; 3) Priya shares prompt set and p95 targets by 9/18; 4) Samir confirms networking constraints by 9/20; 5) schedule security deep-dive next week.
[15:55] Priya: Good. Thanks everyone.
[15:58] Connor: Thanks, bye.
[16:00] End call

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few mis-heard acronyms (KV cache -> "K-V cash"), occasional speaker attribution errors.
